How do I use an original product photo and a marked-up reference image together for a targeted color edit? Search the web and cite the sources supporting your answer.
Using an original product photo alongside a marked-up reference image is a powerful, precise workflow for product photography and e-commerce. The marked-up reference image serves as a "visual prompt" or strict map, ensuring that color modifications are confined only to target areas (like a specific zipper, fabric panel, or logo) while preserving the natural lighting, shadows, and textures of the original shot. 
Pixelz
 +3
This targeted edit can be achieved through traditional professional workflows or modern AI-assisted pipelines:
Method 1: The AI-Assisted Reference Image Pipeline
Modern photo editors allow you to feed both images into an AI model to constrain the edit precisely without manually drawing complex paths. 
Upload the Original Base: Open your original high-resolution product shot in an AI-powered editor like KrafLayer's Reference Editor or use the Generative Fill pipeline in Adobe Photoshop. 
Isolate the Marked-Up Region: Use your selection tools (like the Object Selection tool) to map out the exact areas highlighted on your marked-up reference image. 
YouTube
·Graphd Tutorials
 +1
Inject the Reference: In the selection's contextual taskbar, choose to attach a reference image. Upload your tightly cropped reference image or color swatch. 
Phlearn
 +2
Set Intent to "Object" or "Swap": Ensure the tool is set to focus strictly on the object properties rather than the whole frame background. The AI will transfer the exact sheen, fabric texture, and hue from the reference while respecting the original lighting structure. 
YouTube
·PHLEARN
 +3
Method 2: The Manual Precision Masking Pipeline (Photoshop)
For maximum commercial control over exact hexadecimal alignment, use non-destructive adjustment layers to match the marked-up reference. 
ScreenSnap Pro
 +2
Step 1: Map Selections from the Markup
Open your original photo. Look at your marked-up reference image to see exactly which parts need editing. Use the Pen Tool or Quick Selection Tool to cut out those target parts from the original photo, and save them as separate layer masks. 
Pixelz
 +1
Step 2: Sample Key Tonal Values
Place your reference photo in the document workspace. If matching complex tones (like metallic finishes or fabrics), use the Lasso Tool to sample a dark shadow, a midtone, and a highlight directly from the target color zone on the reference photo. Apply an Average Blur filter over those samples to find the pure target hex codes. 
YouTube
·Adobe Asia Pacific
 +1
Step 3: Remap the Tones
Clip a Curves Adjustment Layer to your original object layer. Double-click the shadow, midtone, and highlight eyedroppers inside the Curves panel to pick up the respective averaged colors from your reference image. Click the corresponding areas on your original product photo to snap its color values directly to the target scheme. 
YouTube
·Big Smile Editing
 +1
Step 4: Refine with Selective Color & Opacity
For flat or simple color swaps, clip a Hue/Saturation or Selective Color adjustment layer to your isolated product mask. Target the specific color channel and manipulate the sliders until it lines up with the markup. Drop the opacity of your adjustment layer slightly (often 50% to 80%) to let the original product's organic highlights bleed through, keeping the edit realistic.
